[1.1] s1:
  p.1 §Abstract: "Methods: We randomised 412 adults aged 50 to 79 with painful knee osteoarthritis to the home exercise programme or usual care at six community clinics." #QM7KBP556Y
  p.2 §2 Methods: "Participants were recruited from six community clinics between March 2023 and February 2024. Eligible adults were aged 50 to 79, had knee pain on most days for at least three months, and had radiographic evidence of osteoarthritis.   p.4 §3 Results: "Benefits were smaller among participants aged 70 and over, in whom the difference in pain was 0.6 points. Benefits did not differ by sex. However, the age subgroup analysis was not pre-specified, and its confidence interval included zero." #6425AZNVZY

ask: Was the BRISK programme effective for older adults?
rows.text:
s1 = Research/BRISK trial report.pdf @adc17a3fac6d
[1] ranked: 11 sentences, 1/5 matching files; 3 more matched (Abstract 2, 2 Methods 1); a larger "budget" shows more
[1.1] s1:
  p.1 §Abstract: "Background: Knee osteoarthritis is a leading cause of pain and disability in older adults." #85BT73MH79
  p.1: "Methods: We randomised 412 adults aged 50 to 79 with painful knee osteoarthritis to the home exercise programme or usual care at six community clinics." #QM7KBP556Y
  p.2 §2 Methods: "Eligible adults were aged 50 to 79, had knee pain on most days for at least three months, and had radiographic evidence of osteoarthritis." #149HFE1TK2
  p.2: "Participants were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio, stratified by clinic, to the home exercise programme (n=206) or usual care (n=206)." #GS0CMJ1PPZ
  p.2 §2.5 Statistical analysis: "No interim analysis of effectiveness was planned." #SPB20DZM9A
  p.3 §3 Results: "We screened 1,083 people, of whom 671 were not eligible or declined: 288 had pain on fewer than half of days, 141 had a joint replacement planned, 97 could not commit to the programme and 145 declined for other reasons." #7XFM4Q5887
  p.3: "Adherence to the programme was 71% over 12 weeks, measured as the share of prescribed sessions recorded in diaries." #T11G9KS59R
  p.5 §4 Discussion: "A home exercise programme reduced knee pain at 12 weeks by more than the minimal clinically important difference, but the effect waned by 24 weeks as adherence declined." #VA37CPF61K
  p.5: "The programme required little staff time: two physiotherapist visits and a booklet. If its short-term benefit can be sustained, it could be offered in primary care at modest cost. Participants who completed most sessions reported the largest improvements, but this comparison is not randomised and may reflect healthier participants adhering more." #A02743P14E

ask: What did the Halden Vale stream buffer monitoring find?
rows.text:
s1 = Studies/Halden Vale buffer monitoring report 2021-2024.pdf @04c4bf73ceac
[1] s1 text:
  p.1 Riparian Buffer Restoration and Stream Water Quality in the Halden Vale
  p.1 Final monitoring report, 2021 to 2024. Prepared by the monitoring team of the Halden Vale Rivers Trust for the Halden Catchment Partnership. Report HVRT-MR-25-02, March 2025.
  p.1 Reviewed by the Partnership's technical group in February 2025. Distribution: Partnership members, participating landowners and the regulator's catchment team.
  p.1 Diffuse pollution from livestock farming is the main pressure on the tributaries of the River Halden. Between January and March 2022 the Halden Catchment Partnership fenced cattle and sheep out of six tributary reaches and planted native broadleaf woodland buffers 10 to 30 metres wide along both banks. We sampled these six restored reaches and six matched control reaches every month from January 2021 to December 2024 in a before-after-control-impact (BACI) design, comparing the 2021 baseline year with 2024, the third growing season after planting. Mean nitrate-N concentrations at restored reaches fell by 31% between 2021 and 2024, while concentrations at control reaches changed little. Total phosphorus and storm-event turbidity also declined at restored reaches, and the mean macroinvertebrate community index rose by 0.7 points. Responses were strongest where buffers were at least 20 metres wide. We conclude that woodland buffers of this width are an effective way to reduce nitrate in lowland livestock catchments, and we recommend widening buffers narrower than 20 metres where land can be secured.
  p.1 Keywords: riparian buffer; diffuse pollution; nitrate; phosphorus; turbidity; stream temperature; macroinvertebrates; BACI design.
  p.2 The River Halden drains about 21,000 hectares of lowland farmland, roughly two thirds of it grazed grassland. Its tributaries have failed their nutrient standards in every classification since 2015, mainly because nitrate and phosphorus are washed from fields and released where livestock have direct access to the channel. Riparian buffers, strips of permanent vegetation between farmland and the stream, are widely promoted as a low-cost remedy because they intercept runoff, take up nutrients, stabilise banks and shade the water. Their performance in practice varies a great deal, however, and few schemes have been monitored for long enough, or against suitable controls, to separate the effect of the buffer from changes in weather and farming.
  p.2 In 2021 the Partnership agreed to fund buffer planting on six tributary reaches and asked the Trust to find out whether water quality and stream ecology improved as a result. This report presents the full four years of monitoring. It addresses three questions: whether nutrient concentrations and turbidity fell at restored reaches relative to controls; whether conditions for stream invertebrates improved; and whether the response depended on the width of the buffer.

  p.1 Riparian Buffer Restoration and Stream Water Quality in the Halden Vale
  p.1 Final monitoring report, 2021 to 2024. Prepared by the monitoring team of the Halden Vale Rivers Trust for the Halden Catchment Partnership. Report HVRT-MR-25-02, March 2025.
  p.1 Reviewed by the Partnership's technical group in February 2025. Distribution: Partnership members, participating landowners and the regulator's catchment team.
  p.1 Diffuse pollution from livestock farming is the main pressure on the tributaries of the River Halden. Between January and March 2022 the Halden Catchment Partnership fenced cattle and sheep out of six tributary reaches and planted native broadleaf woodland buffers 10 to 30 metres wide along both banks. We sampled these six restored reaches and six matched control reaches every month from January 2021 to December 2024 in a before-after-control-impact (BACI) design, comparing the 2021 baseline year with 2024, the third growing season after planting. Mean nitrate-N concentrations at restored reaches fell by 31% between 2021 and 2024, while concentrations at control reaches changed little. Total phosphorus and storm-event turbidity also declined at restored reaches, and the mean macroinvertebrate community index rose by 0.7 points. Responses were strongest where buffers were at least 20 metres wide. We conclude that woodland buffers of this width are an effective way to reduce nitrate in lowland livestock catchments, and we recommend widening buffers narrower than 20 metres where land can be secured.
  p.1 Keywords: riparian buffer; diffuse pollution; nitrate; phosphorus; turbidity; stream temperature; macroinvertebrates; BACI design.
  p.2 The River Halden drains about 21,000 hectares of lowland farmland, roughly two thirds of it grazed grassland. Its tributaries have failed their nutrient standards in every classification since 2015, mainly because nitrate and phosphorus are washed from fields and released where livestock have direct access to the channel. Riparian buffers, strips of permanent vegetation between farmland and the stream, are widely promoted as a low-cost remedy because they intercept runoff, take up nutrients, stabilise banks and shade the water. Their performance in practice varies a great deal, however, and few schemes have been monitored for long enough, or against suitable controls, to separate the effect of the buffer from changes in weather and farming.
  p.2 In 2021 the Partnership agreed to fund buffer planting on six tributary reaches and asked the Trust to find out whether water quality and stream ecology improved as a result. This report presents the full four years of monitoring. It addresses three questions: whether nutrient concentrations and turbidity fell at restored reaches relative to controls; whether conditions for stream invertebrates improved; and whether the response depended on the width of the buffer.

[1] s1 text:
  p.1 Evaluation of the Northfold Community Pharmacy Stop-Smoking Programme
  p.1 Twelve-month results of a cluster-randomised trial. Final report to Northfold Council Public Health, November 2024. Prepared by the Northfold Health Services Evaluation Unit.
  p.1 Background: Most smokers who try to stop do so without professional help, and specialist stop-smoking clinics reach few of them. Community pharmacies are open long hours and are visited by many smokers, which makes them a promising place to offer structured support.
  p.1 Methods: Twenty-four community pharmacies were randomly allocated to deliver the programme (12 pharmacies) or usual care (12 pharmacies). The programme offered six weekly one-to-one sessions with a trained pharmacy adviser and up to 12 weeks of free varenicline or combination nicotine replacement therapy. Usual care consisted of brief advice and a referral to the council's telephone quitline. The primary outcome was continuous abstinence from smoking at 52 weeks, confirmed by an exhaled carbon monoxide reading below 10 parts per million.
  p.1 Results: Between March 2022 and February 2023, 2,310 adult smokers enrolled, 1,212 at programme pharmacies and 1,098 at usual-care pharmacies. At 52 weeks, 14.2% of programme participants and 8.9% of usual-care participants were abstinent (adjusted odds ratio 1.71, 95% confidence interval 1.26 to 2.32). The programme also increased validated abstinence at four weeks.
  p.1 Conclusions: Structured support from a trained pharmacy adviser, with free stop-smoking medicine, increased long-term quitting compared with brief advice. Community pharmacies are a practical setting for stop-smoking support in Northfold.
  p.2 About 17% of adults in Northfold smoke, above the regional average, and smoking remains the largest single cause of the gap in life expectancy between the most and least deprived parts of the district. The council's specialist stop-smoking clinic sees around 600 smokers a year, a small fraction of those who try to quit. In 2021 the council commissioned a pharmacy-based programme to reach more smokers and asked the Evaluation Unit to test it against usual care before deciding whether to extend it across the district.
  p.2 Evidence on pharmacy-delivered support is mixed. A national audit of pharmacy stop-smoking services found an average four-week quit rate of 35%, although fewer than half of the reported quits were confirmed by carbon monoxide testing (Lomax, 2019). In a cluster trial in 16 pharmacies in Tayford, Ridley and colleagues (2020) reported continuous abstinence at 52 weeks of 11.5% with behavioural support plus nicotine replacement therapy, against 7.2% with brief advice.

[1.1] s1 text:
  para 1 Briefing memo: pharmacy stop-smoking programme
  para 2 To: Director of Public Health. From: Tobacco Control Lead. Date: 9 December 2024.
  para 4 This memo summarises the final evaluation report on the community pharmacy stop-smoking programme and asks you to approve extending the programme to all pharmacies in Northfold from April 2025.
  para 6 The programme was tested in a cluster-randomised trial in which 12 pharmacies delivered it and 12 provided usual care, meaning brief advice and a referral to the telephone quitline. Programme participants were offered six weekly sessions with a trained pharmacy adviser and up to 12 weeks of free stop-smoking medicine. In total, 2,310 smokers took part between March 2022 and February 2023.
  para 7 What the evaluation found
  para 8 The programme substantially increased short-term quitting. Four weeks after their quit date, 41.6% of programme participants had stopped smoking, confirmed by a breath test, against 27.3% in usual care.
  para 9 The longer-term result is the one that matters most. At 12 months, 16.4% of programme participants were still not smoking, confirmed by a carbon monoxide breath test, compared with 8.9% of those who received usual care. The evaluation team's adjusted odds ratio for this comparison was 1.71.
  para 10 Smokers aged 60 and over did especially well, with around one in five still smoke-free at 12 months. Nearly two thirds of participants (63%) attended at least four of the six sessions, and no serious side effects were linked to the programme.
  para 11 The programme also reached the people we most need to reach: 38% of programme participants lived in the most deprived fifth of areas in the district.
  para 13 Approve extension of the programme to all 41 community pharmacies in Northfold from April 2025. The 17 pharmacies that did not take part in the trial will need their staff trained before then, and the two-day adviser course can be run in February and March 2025.
  para 15 Demand for adviser time may exceed capacity in the busiest town-centre pharmacies. Supply arrangements for varenicline need to be confirmed with the local pharmaceutical committee. Quit rates in routine services are usually lower than in trials, so outcomes should be monitored quarterly during the first year.

[2.1] s2 text:
  p.1 Evaluation of the Northfold Community Pharmacy Stop-Smoking Programme
  p.1 Twelve-month results of a cluster-randomised trial. Final report to Northfold Council Public Health, November 2024. Prepared by the Northfold Health Services Evaluation Unit.
  p.1 Background: Most smokers who try to stop do so without professional help, and specialist stop-smoking clinics reach few of them. Community pharmacies are open long hours and are visited by many smokers, which makes them a promising place to offer structured support.
  p.1 Methods: Twenty-four community pharmacies were randomly allocated to deliver the programme (12 pharmacies) or usual care (12 pharmacies). The programme offered six weekly one-to-one sessions with a trained pharmacy adviser and up to 12 weeks of free varenicline or combination nicotine replacement therapy. Usual care consisted of brief advice and a referral to the council's telephone quitline. The primary outcome was continuous abstinence from smoking at 52 weeks, confirmed by an exhaled carbon monoxide reading below 10 parts per million.
  p.1 Results: Between March 2022 and February 2023, 2,310 adult smokers enrolled, 1,212 at programme pharmacies and 1,098 at usual-care pharmacies. At 52 weeks, 14.2% of programme participants and 8.9% of usual-care participants were abstinent (adjusted odds ratio 1.71, 95% confidence interval 1.26 to 2.32). The programme also increased validated abstinence at four weeks.
  p.1 Conclusions: Structured support from a trained pharmacy adviser, with free stop-smoking medicine, increased long-term quitting compared with brief advice. Community pharmacies are a practical setting for stop-smoking support in Northfold.
  p.2 About 17% of adults in Northfold smoke, above the regional average, and smoking remains the largest single cause of the gap in life expectancy between the most and least deprived parts of the district. The council's specialist stop-smoking clinic sees around 600 smokers a year, a small fraction of those who try to quit. In 2021 the council commissioned a pharmacy-based programme to reach more smokers and asked the Evaluation Unit to test it against usual care before deciding whether to extend it across the district.
  p.2 Evidence on pharmacy-delivered support is mixed. A national audit of pharmacy stop-smoking services found an average four-week quit rate of 35%, although fewer than half of the reported quits were confirmed by carbon monoxide testing (Lomax, 2019). In a cluster trial in 16 pharmacies in Tayford, Ridley and colleagues (2020) reported continuous abstinence at 52 weeks of 11.5% with behavioural support plus nicotine replacement therapy, against 7.2% with brief advice.

```
# Kestle Bay heat pump programme: board meeting notes, 14 November 2024

## Kestle Bay heat pump programme: board meeting notes, 14 November 2024

Present: Rosa Penhallow (chair), Daniel Kitto, Meera Joshi, Tom Rowe and Ellen Vosper (programme manager). Apologies: Gareth Lobb.

## Progress

Ellen reported that the first phase closed in September with 214 installations. Installers now report a median of 9 weeks between the home survey and the installation date, down from 14 weeks in the first year of the programme.

## Installers

Brightwater Heating withdrew from the programme in August because of staff shortages, leaving Pellow and Sons as the only appointed installer. The board agreed to run a new tender in January to appoint at least one more installer before phase two begins.

## Complaints

Six formal complaints were received in 2024, four of them about installation delays and two about the condition of gardens after outdoor units were fitted. All have been resolved.

## Phase two

The board agreed a target of 150 further installations by March 2026, with priority for homes heated by oil or bottled gas. It also agreed to cap the householder contribution at GBP 4,000 for households receiving means-tested benefits, with the society's hardship fund meeting the rest of the cost.

## Actions

Ellen to draft the installer tender by 12 December. Daniel to ask the Coastal Communities Net Zero Fund whether the grant can stay at GBP 6,000 per home in phase two. Meera to update the website with the new waiting times.
```

[1] s1 text:
  p.1 Borrowing instead of buying: evaluation of the Brackenford Library of Things pilot, April 2023 to March 2025
  p.1 Northfold Social Research, for Brackenford Libraries. Final report, September 2025.
  p.1 The Brackenford Library of Things lends household tools and equipment from three branch libraries for a small fee. This report evaluates the first two years of the pilot, from April 2023 to March 2025, using membership and loan records, a survey of borrowers and the checks that staff make when items are returned. Almost 2,000 residents registered as borrowers, and loans grew by 64 percent between the first and second years. Borrowers reported modest savings, and most items came back in good condition. Registrations from deprived neighbourhoods were roughly in line with their share of the town's population. We recommend that the scheme continues, with changes to how damage is recorded and how new items are chosen.
  p.1 Libraries of things apply the familiar library model to objects that households need only occasionally, such as drills, gazebos and sewing machines. Their supporters argue that borrowing saves money, reduces the number of rarely used items that people buy, and brings people into libraries who would not otherwise visit.
  p.1 Brackenford Libraries opened its Library of Things in April 2023 with a grant of GBP 96,000 from the Halden Foundation, which also funded this evaluation. The pilot ran from three of the town's seven branch libraries: Central, Eastgate and Millbrook.
  p.2 Items could be reserved online and collected from any of the three branches, and loans lasted up to seven days. This report sets out what the pilot achieved against the aims agreed with the funder: to reach a broad range of residents, to build regular use, to save households money and to reduce waste. Section 2 summarises earlier evaluations of similar schemes, Section 3 describes our methods, Section 4 presents the results, and Sections 5 to 7 discuss them.
  p.2 Published evaluations of libraries of things are few, and most describe a single scheme in its first years. A survey of 14 schemes in England found a median of 1,150 registered borrowers per scheme after two years of operation, with wide variation by town size (Carraway Trust, 2022). The same survey reported a median household saving of GBP 60 a year among borrowers who answered its questionnaire.
  p.2 Repeat borrowing, the share of borrowers who borrow more than once, is often used as a sign that a scheme has become part of household routines. It was 34 percent at the Harwick Tool Library in its second year (Pemberton and Shah, 2021) and 39 percent at the Otterburn Share Shed (Lindqvist, 2023). Damage rates reported by tool libraries usually fall between 2 and 5 percent of loans, with power tools at the upper end of that range (Odum, 2020).

[1.1] s1:
  p.1 §Abstract: "The Brackenford Library of Things lends household tools and equipment from three branch libraries for a small fee." #44VF3B97F7
  p.1: "Registrations from deprived neighbourhoods were roughly in line with their share of the town's population." #VXCG96906M
  p.1 §1 Introduction: "The pilot ran from three of the town's seven branch libraries: Central, Eastgate and Millbrook." #6CHF9H1KD9
  p.2 §2 Previous studies: "A survey of 14 schemes in England found a median of 1,150 registered borrowers per scheme after two years of operation, with wide variation by town size (Carraway Trust, 2022)." #15E51E8MA0
  p.6 §4.4 Avoided purchases and emissions: "Applying these answers to the 1,820 combinations of member and item type in the loan records, we estimate that the pilot avoided the purchase of about 1,130 items with a combined weight of 14.6 tonnes. These avoided purchases correspond to around 38 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent over the two years, mostly from power tools and garden machinery." #1VM77WRSEE
  p.7 §4.5 Condition of returned items: "Damage was most common for power tools and garden equipment (Table 3)." #8K5STQJS2Q

  p.1: "Evaluation of the Kestle Bay Community Heat Pump Programme, 2022 to 2024" #45YT6FV30K
  p.1: "Tressider Energy Research, for Kestle Bay Community Energy." #1PGFNGDYWT
  p.1 §Abstract: "Kestle Bay Community Energy, a community benefit society, ran a programme between October 2022 and September 2024 to help owner-occupiers on the Kestle Bay peninsula replace fossil-fuel heating with air-source heat pumps." #0GEJZ2GD4R
  p.1: "Household energy bills fell by 21 percent on average after installation, and homes were warmer in winter. Emissions from heating fell substantially. Most residents were satisfied with their systems, although around one in ten reported a fault in the first year." #1QZ65VZK9B
  p.3 §3.1 The programme: "Households that went ahead received a grant of GBP 6,000 towards the installed cost and could borrow the remainder through an interest-free loan arranged by the society. Two installers were appointed after a tender in the summer of 2022." #TDQFQSV4VW
  p.3 §3.2 Data sources: "Temperature loggers were placed in the living rooms of 48 homes that volunteered, recording every thirty minutes for one winter before and one winter after installation." #2FCXHR6ADH
  p.4 §4.1 Uptake: "Between October 2022 and September 2024, 597 households registered an interest, 318 received a home survey and 214 had a heat pump installed. This conversion rate of 36 percent from registration to installation is above that reported for the Lowmoor scheme." #3XKX7XH57R
  p.5 §4.2 Energy bills: "Complete meter data for a full year before and after installation were available for 162 homes." #02CCD73Q3X
  p.5: "For the 52 homes without complete meter data, installers' estimates suggest similar savings, but these could not be checked." #2CGVZMJAP4
  p.6 §4.3 Indoor temperatures: "In the 48 homes with temperature loggers, the mean living-room temperature from December to February rose by 1.6 deg C, from 17.9 deg C before installation to 19.5 deg C after. This gain was largest in homes that had relied on electric storage heaters, which had often been the coldest before the programme." #DTZSPYAD6W
  p.6 §4.4 Emissions: "Across all 214 installations, this amounts to about 490 tonnes a year." #T88Z12264V

  p.8 §7 Conclusions: "The Kestle Bay programme shows that a community energy group can deliver heat pumps at scale in an area with many older and off-grid homes." #BS99VMK03T
